clinical: The third molars, or wisdom teeth, erupt last and often lack room in the jaw. They can become impacted and may need to be removed.
Bacteria in plaque turn sugar into acid that dissolves enamel. Once decay passes through enamel into dentin, it spreads faster and can reach the pulp.
Decay or injury can inflame and kill the pulp, causing toothache. Root canal treatment removes the pulp and fills the canals.

Periodontitis destroys the periodontal ligament and alveolar bone, so teeth loosen and can be lost. It usually develops from gingivitis, inflammation of the gums that can be reversed by removing plaque.
The thin white line of alveolar bone around each root (the lamina dura) shows on dental X-rays. Thinning or loss of that line is a sign of bone loss from periodontal disease.

Tooth – Nerves & vessels.description: The inferior alveolar nerve, artery and vein run together in the mandibular canal of the lower jaw. Small dental branches enter each tooth through its apical foramen to reach the pulp. The nerve carries sensation such as pain, the artery supplies blood to the pulp and the vein drains it.
clinical: An injection of local anaesthetic near the mandibular foramen (an inferior alveolar nerve block) numbs the lower teeth on that side.
Damage to the inferior alveolar nerve, for example during removal of a lower wisdom tooth, can cause numbness of the lower lip and chin.

Tooth – Coronal dentin-pulp histology (1.description: Dentin is the hard layer under the enamel, and it is pierced by fine tubules. Odontoblast cells line the pulp and send processes into those tubules, so living cells reach into the hard tissue. Between the odontoblasts and the mature dentin lies predentin, which is not yet mineralised, and the pulp inside is soft connective tissue with fibroblasts.
clinical: When enamel wears away or gums recede and expose the root, the open dentin tubules let cold, sweet or touch stimuli reach the pulp, causing sensitivity.
When decay or wear irritates the pulp, odontoblasts lay down extra reparative dentin to wall off the damage.

parts.description: Dentine is the hard, pale tissue that makes up the bulk of the tooth, lying under the enamel in the crown and under the cementum on the root. It is about 70% mineral by weight, and its matrix is pierced by tubules containing odontoblast processes, so it is living tissue. When dentine is exposed, cold and sweet stimuli move fluid in the tubules and excite the pulp nerves, causing sensitivity. Odontoblasts keep depositing secondary dentine throughout life, slowly narrowing the pulp chamber.

The pulp chamber is the soft connective-tissue core of the crown, filling the cavity under the enamel and dentine and reaching up into pulp horns beneath each cusp. Its outer edge is lined by odontoblasts, and it contains fibroblasts, blood vessels, lymphatics and nerves, including fibres that carry sharp pain and fibres that carry dull, throbbing pain. Being enclosed in rigid dentine, inflamed pulp has little room to swell. The chamber gradually shrinks with age as secondary dentine is laid down.

The root canals are the narrow channels that continue the pulp cavity down through each root, from the pulp chamber to the apical foramen at the tip. A lower first molar's mesial root usually has two canals (mesiobuccal and mesiolingual), and its distal root has one or two. Nerves and blood vessels enter and leave through the apical foramen. Root canal treatment (endodontics) removes infected pulp, cleans and shapes the canals, and seals them with gutta-percha to save a tooth with irreversible pulpitis.

The apical foramen is the small opening at the tip of each root, where the root canal connects with the periodontal tissues around the root. Blood vessels and nerves pass through it to and from the pulp, and its position often differs from the geometric tip of the root. In a necrotic, infected pulp, infection can spread out through this opening into the tissues around the root tip, causing periapical inflammation or an abscess.

Cortical bone of the mandible is the dense compact bone forming the outer (buccal) and inner (lingual) plates of the jaw and its lower border. These plates enclose the spongy bone that holds the tooth sockets, so the cortex gives the jaw its strength and resists the forces of chewing. On radiographs it appears as a dense white outline, and its thickness varies between people and between sites.

Cancellous (spongy) bone is the porous, lattice-like bone lying between the cortical plates of the jaw, made of trabeculae (thin bony bars) with marrow in the spaces between them. It supports the tooth sockets, and it forms the interradicular septum between the roots of a molar and the interdental septa between neighbouring teeth. Small dental branches of the inferior alveolar nerve and vessels run through its marrow towards the root apices. On radiographs it looks less dense than the surrounding cortex.

The mandibular canal is a bony tunnel running through the mandible below the tooth roots, carrying the inferior alveolar nerve, artery and vein. It begins at the mandibular foramen on the inner side of the ramus and gives off small dental branches to the lower teeth. Near the premolars the nerve divides, with the mental nerve leaving through the mental foramen and the incisive nerve continuing forward within the bone. On radiographs the canal appears as a dark band with thin white borders beneath the molar roots.

The inferior alveolar nerve is a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (V3) that enters the mandibular foramen on the inner side of the ramus. It is mainly sensory and runs forward in the mandibular canal, giving off dental branches that form a plexus supplying the lower teeth and their pulp. Near the premolars it divides into the mental nerve, which supplies the chin and lower lip, and the incisive nerve, which continues forward in the bone.

The inferior alveolar artery is a branch of the first part of the maxillary artery, and it enters the mandibular foramen alongside the nerve. It runs in the mandibular canal and gives off dental branches that form a plexus of vessels supplying the lower teeth, their pulp and the surrounding bone. Its terminal branch, the mental artery, leaves through the mental foramen to supply the chin and lower lip.

The inferior alveolar vein runs with the artery and nerve in the mandibular canal, receiving blood from the dental veins that form a plexus around the lower tooth roots. It drains the lower teeth, their pulp and the surrounding jaw bone, and it leaves the mandible to empty into the pterygoid venous plexus in the infratemporal fossa. The pterygoid plexus in turn drains into the maxillary vein.

The gingiva is the part of the oral mucosa that overlies the alveolar bone and surrounds the necks of the teeth. The free gingiva forms a collar around each tooth, while the attached gingiva is firmly bound to the underlying bone and cementum. Its outer surface is keratinised or parakeratinised, often stippled, and the shallow gingival sulcus ends where the junctional epithelium attaches the gum to the tooth by hemidesmosomes.

The incisor crown is the enamel-covered part of the tooth above the cementoenamel junction, shaped like a chisel with a straight, thin incisal edge for cutting food. Each quadrant has a central and a lateral incisor, eight in all in the permanent dentition, and the flat incisal edge tells them apart from the pointed canines and cusped premolars.

The incisor root is the single, conical root that lies below the cementoenamel junction, coated with cementum and held in its socket by the periodontal ligament. Being a single tapering root, it anchors the chisel-shaped crown firmly in the front of the jaw, so the biting forces of cutting food are carried down into the alveolar bone.

The canine crown is the enamel-covered part of the tooth above the cementoenamel junction, with a single, pointed cusp for piercing and tearing food. There is one canine in each quadrant, four in all in the adult, set at the corner of the arch between the incisors and premolars. It is also called the cuspid, and its single cusp distinguishes it from the chisel-shaped incisors.

The canine root is the longest root of any tooth in the mouth, coated with cementum and held deep in its socket by the periodontal ligament. In the upper jaw the root extends high into the maxilla, beneath the orbit, which is why the upper canine is called the 'eye tooth'. This long root makes the canine a stable anchor at the corner of the dental arch, resisting the sideways forces of tearing food.

The premolar crown is the enamel-covered part of the tooth above the cementoenamel junction, with two cusps: a large buccal cusp and a smaller lingual cusp, used for crushing and grinding food. There are two premolars in each quadrant, eight in all in the adult, and they replace the deciduous molars, as there are no deciduous premolars.

The premolar root is usually a single root, coated with cementum and held in its socket by the periodontal ligament. The upper first premolar is the common exception, often having two roots, one buccal and one palatal, which share the load of biting and chewing.

The molar crown is the broad, enamel-covered part of the tooth above the cementoenamel junction, with a wide occlusal surface carrying four or five cusps for grinding food. There are three molars in each quadrant, twelve in all in the adult including the four third molars or wisdom teeth. The first permanent molars erupt at about six years, behind the deciduous teeth, and are often mistaken for milk teeth.

The molar neck is the constricted zone where the broad crown of a molar meets its roots, at the cementoenamel junction. Just below this line the root trunk divides to form the two roots of a lower molar or the three roots of an upper molar, a point called the furcation. Gum recession exposes the cementum here, which makes this area vulnerable to root caries.

The molar roots are the cementum-coated roots that anchor the molar in its socket, held by the periodontal ligament. Lower molars have two roots, a mesial and a distal, while upper molars usually have three: two buccal roots and one palatal root. Their multiple roots give a large molar a wide, stable base to withstand the heavy forces of chewing.

Tubular dentine is the mineralised bulk of the tooth's hard tissue, pierced by fine dentinal tubules. Each tubule contains a cytoplasmic odontoblast process, so the dentine is living tissue, and the tubules run outwards from the pulp, slightly S-shaped in the crown. In a ground section they appear as fine, parallel channels running through the hard matrix.

Predentin is the unmineralised layer of dentine matrix lying between the odontoblasts and the fully mineralised dentine. Its matrix is mainly organic, chiefly type I collagen laid down by the odontoblasts, and it mineralises only at the mineralisation front where it meets mature dentine. In a stained section it forms a narrow, paler band beside the odontoblasts, marking the zone where new dentine is being formed.

Odontoblast bodies are the tall, columnar cells forming a single, palisade-like layer along the pulp border of the predentin. Each odontoblast sends one long cytoplasmic process into the dentinal tubules, which is the living contact between the cell and the mineralised dentine. In a stained section, look for a regular row of tall cells lining the pulp, with their processes seen as fine threads pointing into the dentine.

Odontoblast nuclei are the oval nuclei of the odontoblast cells, which sit at the pulp end of each tall cell, away from the dentine. Packed closely together, they form a regular row of dark-stained nuclei that makes the odontoblast layer easy to spot. Unlike the scattered, elongated nuclei of pulp fibroblasts deeper in the pulp, they lie in an orderly palisade at the pulp border.

The pulp connective-tissue matrix is the soft ground substance and fine collagen fibres that fill the pulp between its cells, vessels and nerves. It is rich in proteoglycans and glycosaminoglycans, which hold water, and it contains collagen types I and III and reticular fibres that give the pulp its supporting framework. In routine stained sections it looks pale and loosely textured, like other loose connective tissue.

Pulp fibroblasts are the main resident cells of the dental pulp, lying scattered through its loose connective tissue between the vessels and nerves. They make the collagen and ground substance that maintain the pulp matrix, and they can differentiate into odontoblast-like cells when the pulp is injured. Under the microscope they are recognised by spindle-shaped or stellate cell bodies among the fine collagen fibres.

Fibroblast nuclei are the oval-to-elongated nuclei of pulp fibroblasts, scattered through the pulp matrix away from the odontoblast layer. They are paler and less densely packed than the odontoblast nuclei, and they are often aligned with the collagen fibres around them. Recognising them helps separate the cell-rich pulp core from the odontoblast palisade at the pulp border.
